newsitem.title: GERMANY: Top bankers see EMU forging more integration.
newsitem.headline: Top bankers see EMU forging more integration.

text.p: Top international bankers taking part in a conference on European monetary union on Tuesday welcomed the prospect of a single European currency and said the project would foster essential integration.

Rolf Breuer, chairman of Germany's largest bank Deutsche Bank AG, told the Global 24 conference that the world must stop worrying about the changes currency union would bring and instead look at the trade and market advantages it would offer.

"An integrated Europe will have a stronger impact on international capital markets than any individual countries have had," Breuer said in a Frankfurt-based European Monetary Union conference transmitted by video link to Tokyo, London, Milan and New York.
"All the EU countries together represent one of the world's largest economic areas. The single currency will add impetus to European integration."

Industrial Bank of Japan chairman Yoh Kurosawa, speaking on a video-link from Tokyo, said Japanese investors were interested in investment in the euro block and looked forward to the euro launch, as planned for January 1999.
"We Japanese welcome very much a strong Europe, a strong European currency," he said.

Traditionally, Japanese investors had bought U.S., New Zealand and Australian bonds, but Kurosawa noted that the yen had appreciated against those currencies in the past three weeks and investors were always on the lookout for alternatives.
"If you have a huge euro bond market that would be an opportunity for investment. We welcome that opportunity."
At the same time, Kurosawa urged EU states to get to grips with the stubbornly high levels of joblessness in the region.
"We all know that European countries are suffering from unemployment and I think this is the first target," he said.
He also said the Japanese business community did not expect the euro to compete with the Japanese yen.
Bankers anticipated a gradual shift in international investments practices as a result of the euro's launch.
Kurosawa said a strong euro would diminish the significance of the dollar as a reserve currency, which would lead to more stability on currencies worldwide.

European Commission president Jacques Santer said the euro would open up new opportunities for European Union exporters and would play an increasingly important role in international trade and world capital markets.

"There is no reason to expect that the euro exchange rate will be either too strong or too weak against any other currency. It is the policy mix in the euro area and relative to that of major partners that is relevant," Santer said.
Sound policies should result in a stable euro, he said.
"I therefore conclude that Europe is heading for a strong and stable currency that will fully deserve its place among the major international currencies."
Breuer, a well established champion of EMU, said one of its chief advantages would be to encourage a complete and essential reshuffle in European equity markets.

"Europe's fragmented equity markets will develop into the world's third largest equity market thanks to EMU," he said. "There is no place and no need for 32 stock exchanges and 23 futures and options exchanges. It will be the survival of the fittest."
Breuer warned against any efforts to undermine the euro project.
"Instead of worrying about the new developing market ... one must start appreciating the opportunities associated with the euro," he said. --Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
